source_quotes.quote: The gain is not attributed to the traces alone. The hand-written seed, Claude 5 Opus (which writes the primitives), and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (which mines the rules) all contribute, and neither frontier model is a blank slate about customer service or tool use; the ablation that removes the traces and the primitives still reaches 75.9% on Telecom (§ 5.6 ), and that ablation covers Retail and Telecom only. Inference under the program costs 5 to 10 times a vanilla run in FLOPs. All cells but the program’s Telecom cells are single runs, so differences of a few points are not resolved. The synthetic training tasks share the τ 2 \tau^{2} Retail and Telecom domains with the test suites and the LiveMCPBench format with LiveMCPBench, so domain knowledge can pass from the training set into the primitives, the rules, and the fine-tunes. The training tasks and their answers are different from the test tasks; the authors verified this.

We compiled a teacher’s procedure into a program rather than into a student’s weights: primitives authored by a frontier model from clusters of the teacher’s traces, each run by a small frozen model and verified as it runs, assembled by A ∗ over a rule library mined from the same traces under a reference-action objective, and used at inference to write the student’s chain of thought or to check the actions the student proposes. Run in front of three Nemotron base models and on its own, the one program estimates how much of each domain is procedure. On τ 2 \tau^{2} Telecom the estimate is that nearly all of it is: Granite-4.2-8B as the student goes from 43.0% to 91.2%, every Nemotron student reaches 93.3–94.4%, and no other arm passes 58.2%. On τ 2 \tau^{2} Retail the 8B student under the program is within 2.7 points of the Nemotron students; on LiveMCPBench the Nemotron students are 3 to 13 points ahead of it. On those two suites the program is competitive with the best baseline. No weights are updated, the program is the same for every base model, and the spread between base models shrinks where the program does the work. The program was produced once, at 3.0 × 10 19 3.0\times 10^{19} FLOPs, and costs 5 to 10 times a vanilla run to execute. Its output is a program rather than a checkpoint: it can be read at every step, it is the same for every base model, and it can be revised one primitive at a time.

Claude 5 Opus generated the tasks. For retail and telecom it used τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench’s own tools, environment, and policies and wrote new questions against them; for tool-search it used LiveMCPBench’s registry format and wrote new questions against that.

The three suites give different answers. On Telecom the program with Granite-4.2-8B as the student scores 91.2%, every Nemotron student under it 93.3–94.4%, and no other arm above 58.2%; the procedure is nearly the whole result, and on this suite an 8B model is enough to run it. The result is in-domain compositional generalisation: the program is built from synthetic tasks in the benchmark’s own environment, with its tools and policies, and is run on the benchmark’s test tasks, which it has not seen; it is not a claim about transfer to another domain. Telecom is also where the program’s student runs longest, about 40 turns per task against about 9 on Retail. On Retail the program with Granite as the student scores 82.5%, within 2.7 points of the Nemotron students, so there too the choice of student matters little under the program, though the program’s margin over the baselines is small. On LiveMCPBench the program with Granite as the student reaches 42.1% and the Nemotron students are 3.2 to 12.6 points ahead of it; the student’s tool choice and argument binding still count. We read the part of the gap between base models that the program closes as an estimate of how much of that gap is procedure; the program also carries the frontier models’ prior knowledge (§ 5.6 ), so the estimate is an upper bound.

notes_zh: v2原文支持失败反馈后修工具、冻结后测试；当前v2公开范围摘要可保留。
v3主体是固定通用代码与自然语言task skill，每稿人工审核；这是修改对象/分支变化，不能直接继承v2工具自改的accept。
人工审核本身不等于排除：本回执仅确认版本边界，v3主线仍需独立范围意见。
v3回顾旧TaskTools冻结后152/420开发回放通过，且7项工具有场景尺寸捷径；必须留反证，不用新主线成绩改写旧刊。

source_quotes.quote: One command starts a run for one task on one GPU. The loop uses the first ten layouts of evaluation seed 0 (for Generalization tasks, five standard and five cluttered, which share tools) and proceeds layout by layout. The acting agent attempts the layout with the current tools. On success, the optimizer agent reads the trajectory and adds a short entry to playbook.md on which tools worked and why. On failure, it reads the command log, the camera frames of every command and the current tool code. It writes a diagnosis to skill.md and adds or fixes a tool. A delivery check then verifies that files are complete, tools load, and the interface text names neither the task nor its objects; if the check fails the edit is reverted. The simulator is restarted and the same layout is attempted again, up to five edits per layout. After the tenth layout the optimizer consolidates its notes, the tool set is frozen and tested once more with no optimizer, on the ten development layouts and on ten new layouts ( Section 4.1 ).

Skills are drafted by an analysis agent, which reads the records of earlier runs of a group of related tasks, including every cell, output and image, and marks the evidence behind each claim; a person reviews every draft. A skill may contain only what the agent could observe: no positions read from the simulator, no internal names and no checker thresholds, a constraint enforced by a checking script. The median skill has 39 to 61 lines, depending on the benchmark, and only three of the 205 skills contain code ( Section E.6 ).

Knowledge that a general harness lacks about a task can be supplied either as brief guidance, as in HexaShell, or as an elaborate task-specific toolset. HexaShell-TaskTools, an earlier version of our agent listed as HexaShell-Preview on the RoboDojo leaderboard, takes the latter approach. An acting agent (the Codex command-line agent with GPT-6-Astra) drives the robot through a command line. After each failed episode, an optimizer agent of the same model writes or repairs the task’s tools, with their tests, and the same layout is tried again. Each task was developed for up to 12 hours on the first ten layouts of seed 0, the same development layouts that HexaShell used. The 769 optimizer rounds left 327 task commands in about 78,000 lines of Python, which were then frozen. In RoboDojo’s official evaluation, on a hidden seed with 50 episodes per task, they reach a success rate of 46.9 and a score of 53.2. Table 6 sets this official result against our two test runs of Table 3 , overall and per dimension, with the Open tasks counted as in Table 3 .

The resulting code is large and generalizes poorly. Re-run after freezing, the tools pass only 152 of the 420 development episodes on which they were built (36%). An audit further found object sizes copied from the scenes into the tools of seven tasks, a shortcut that a measurement within the episode should replace. HexaShell, by contrast, keeps no tools for any task. Its 34 RoboDojo skills are plain text, about 2,700 lines in total or about a page per task, each of which a person can read and verify; only three contain code ( Section E.6 ).

Coding agents read a repository, run its tests and fix the code [ 18 , 41 , 82 , 78 ] , and Reflexion [ 68 ] keeps verbal lessons from failed attempts. Voyager [ 73 ] grows a library of code skills while playing Minecraft. Toolformer [ 67 ] learns when to call tools, LATM [ 13 ] and CRAFT [ 85 ] have language models write and retrieve tools, and self-improving systems modify their own programs and retain the changes that raise a score [ 86 , 60 , 52 ] . In robotics, recent harnesses let coding agents program, test and refine robot skills [ 26 , 53 , 80 , 74 , 25 , 72 , 17 , 87 ] , some starting from a few human demonstrations [ 51 , 42 ] . URAI pairs a programming agent that writes motion tools with an execution agent that calls them [ 32 ] . EmbodiedEvo turns physical feedback into code skills and diagnostic lessons [ 45 ] , MEMENTO evolves code policies with a memory of past programs [ 71 ] , and Gao et al . [ 31 ] treat tools, traces and memory as code that a physical coding agent revises. In most of these systems, what is retained for a task is code, as in HexaShell-TaskTools, an earlier version of our agent that wrote and repaired tools for each task ( Section 3.4 ). In HexaShell the code is general and fixed, and what is retained for a task is only a short, reviewed skill in natural language. In this respect it is closer to Reflexion’s verbal lessons than to a skill library.
